lead: Every first-order ODE you meet in an exam belongs to a small number of families, and each family has one standard move. This unit gives you those moves — separable, homogeneous, exact, linear and Bernoulli — plus the theory that says when a solution exists and when it is unique. By the end you can classify an equation, choose the method, carry it to a general or particular solution, and state Picard's theorem without mixing up existence and uniqueness.
about: The unit is about equations in one independent variable x, one unknown y and its first derivative. Chapter 1.1 teaches you to read an equation before solving it: order, degree, linearity, and the higher-degree forms such as Clairaut's. Chapters 1.2 to 1.4 give the three classical moves — splitting variables, the v = y/x substitution for homogeneous equations, and the exactness test with integrating factors. Chapter 1.5 turns the exact-equation idea into the integrating factor e to the power ∫P dx for the linear equation, and 1.6 reduces Bernoulli's equation to that linear case. Chapter 1.7 closes with theory: the Lipschitz condition, Peano's and Picard's theorems, and Picard iteration, which also shows how a solution can fail to exist or to be unique.

chapters.idea: Classify an ODE — order, degree, linearity — because the classification tells you which of the later methods can even apply.
chapters.depth: Define an ordinary differential equation and contrast it in one line with a partial one. Order is the highest derivative present. Degree is the power of that highest derivative once the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives, so fractions and radicals in derivatives must be cleared first. Linearity: a<sub>n</sub>(x)y<sup>(n)</sup> + ... + a<sub>1</sub>(x)y′ + a<sub>0</sub>(x)y = f(x), where y and every derivative appear to power one with no products such as y·y′ and no sin y, e<sup>y</sup> or √y. Give the three working forms of a first-order equation: y′ = f(x, y), M(x, y)dx + N(x, y)dy = 0, and dy/dx = M/N. On examples: y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 0 is order 2, degree 1, linear; (y′)² + y = x is order 1, degree 2, nonlinear; y′ = y² is order 1, degree 1, nonlinear. General solution carries as many arbitrary constants as the order; a particular solution fixes them. Show briefly how a family such as y = ax² + b produces an ODE by eliminating the constants. Some syllabi also list first-order equations of higher degree here: solvable for p, and Clairaut's form y = px + f(p) with p = dy/dx, general solution y = cx + f(c), and a singular solution when x + f′(p) = 0 also holds. Keep Clairaut to a method and one example.

figure.aria: A classification tree splits differential equations by order, then by linearity, with an example of each kind at the leaves.

chapters.example: Classify each equation by order, degree and linearity: (i) (d²y/dx²)³ + x(dy/dx)⁵ = y; (ii) y′ = y² + x; (iii) y = px + p² where p = dy/dx. Then solve (iii). Answers: (i) order 2, degree 3, nonlinear; (ii) order 1, degree 1, nonlinear; (iii) order 1, degree 2, nonlinear. For (iii), differentiate with respect to x: p = p + (x + 2p)dp/dx, so (x + 2p)dp/dx = 0. Either dp/dx = 0 giving p = c and the general solution y = cx + c², or x + 2p = 0 giving p = −x/2 and the singular solution y = −x²/4.
chapters.trap: Degree exists only when the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives. Clear first: (y″)^(1/2) = y squares to y″ = y², so the degree is 1, not 1/2. Linearity is about y and its derivatives, not about x — x²y′ + cos(x)y = 0 is still linear.
chapters.prereq: First-year calculus: derivatives, the chain rule, basic integrals.
chapters.leave: The solving methods are 1.2 to 1.6. Second-order theory, Wronskians and constant coefficients belong to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: If the right side factors as g(x) times h(y), then all the y-terms can go to one side and all the x-terms to the other, and each side integrates alone.
chapters.depth: Standard forms dy/dx = g(x)h(y) and M(x)dx + N(y)dy = 0. Procedure: factor, divide by h(y), integrate both sides, add one constant, then apply any initial condition to get the particular solution. Check separately for constant solutions lost in the division. Work examples that need substitution after separating: y′ = e<sup>x+y</sup>, y′ = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²), and y′ = (x + y + 1)² with v = x + y + 1, which reduces to a separable equation in v. Include three application models with real numbers: Newton's law of cooling, radioactive decay, and simple population growth. One line on the name: the same phrase separation of variables appears again for PDEs in Unit 5, but there it separates two independent variables.

figure.aria: The solution curve y = (1+x)/(1−x) starts at the point (0, 1) and shoots upward as x approaches 1.

chapters.example: Solve dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²) with y(0) = 1. Separate: dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²). Integrate: tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + C. At x = 0, y = 1 gives C = tan⁻¹1 = π/4. So tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + π/4 and y = tan(tan⁻¹x + π/4) = (1 + x)/(1 − x). The solution is valid for x < 1, where it blows up.
chapters.trap: Dividing by h(y) silently drops the constant solutions h(y) = 0. For dy/dx = y² − 1, both y = 1 and y = −1 are solutions the general solution misses. Also find C at the initial point before rearranging, not after.
chapters.prereq: 1.1, plus integration by substitution and partial fractions.
chapters.leave: Equations that need an exactness test go to 1.4; those with the pattern y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) go to 1.5.

chapters.idea: When the right side depends only on the ratio y/x, the substitution v = y/x turns the equation into a separable one in v and x.
chapters.depth: Homogeneous function: f(λx, λy) = λ<sup>n</sup>f(x, y) for every λ > 0, with n the degree. The equation M dx + N dy = 0 is homogeneous when M and N are homogeneous of the same degree. Substitute y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, and the equation becomes x dv/dx = f(v) − v, which separates in v and x. Integrate, then put v = y/x back; answers often sit better in polar form with x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. Include examples with inverse-trig and log answers. Add the reducible case dy/dx = (a<sub>1</sub>x + b<sub>1</sub>y + c<sub>1</sub>)/(a<sub>2</sub>x + b<sub>2</sub>y + c<sub>2</sub>): if a<sub>1</sub>b<sub>2</sub> ≠ a<sub>2</sub>b<sub>1</sub>, shift the origin by X = x − h, Y = y − k with (h, k) solving a<sub>1</sub>h + b<sub>1</sub>k + c<sub>1</sub> = 0 and a<sub>2</sub>h + b<sub>2</sub>k + c<sub>2</sub> = 0; if a<sub>1</sub>b<sub>2</sub> = a<sub>2</sub>b<sub>1</sub>, substitute v = a<sub>1</sub>x + b<sub>1</sub>y instead.

figure.title: Homogeneous to separable
figure.aria: A left-to-right pipeline shows v = y/x converting a homogeneous equation into a separable one and then back to y.

chapters.example: Solve dy/dx = (x + y)/(x − y). Put y = vx: v + x dv/dx = (1 + v)/(1 − v), so x dv/dx = (1 + v²)/(1 − v). Separate: (1 − v)dv/(1 + v²) = dx/x. Integrate: tan⁻¹v − ½ln(1 + v²) = ln|x| + C. With v = y/x this tidies to tan⁻¹(y/x) = ½ln(x² + y²) + C, or in polar form θ = ln r + C.
chapters.trap: y = vx gives dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, not v′x alone. Also check both M and N have the same degree — M = x² + y, N = xy is not homogeneous, and forcing the substitution gives a mess.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 and 1.2 (the separated equation is solved by 1.2).
chapters.leave: Equations that are not exact and have no ratio pattern go to 1.4 for an integrating factor.

chapters.idea: M dx + N dy = 0 is exact when ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x, and then the left side is the total differential of some F(x, y), so the solution is F(x, y) = C.
chapters.depth: State the criterion and justify it in three lines: if F<sub>x</sub> = M and F<sub>y</sub> = N with continuous second partials, then M<sub>y</sub> = F<sub>xy</sub> = F<sub>yx</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>. Solve by either route — integrate M with respect to x and fix the arbitrary function g(y) from N, or the mirror route. Insist on the check that ends every exactness solution. Then integrating factors: when the equation fails the test, look for μ so that μM dx + μN dy = 0 is exact. Give the two standard rules: μ(x) = e<sup>∫R dx</sup> with R = (M<sub>y</sub> − N<sub>x</sub>)/N when R depends on x alone, and μ(y) = e<sup>∫S dy</sup> with S = (N<sub>x</sub> − M<sub>y</sub>)/M when S depends on y alone. Show solution by grouping for simple differentials: y dx + x dy = d(xy), (x dy − y dx)/x² = d(y/x), and the like, kept as a small table. Mention in one line that other integrating factors exist, for example 1/(xM + yN) for a homogeneous equation with xM + yN ≠ 0; only a few universities teach that one.

figure.title: Exact or make it exact
figure.aria: A flowchart tests M_y against N_x and branches to the direct integral or to multiplying by an integrating factor.

chapters.example: (a) Solve (2xy + y²)dx + (x² + 2xy)dy = 0. Here M<sub>y</sub> = 2x + 2y and N<sub>x</sub> = 2x + 2y, so the equation is exact. F = ∫M dx = x²y + xy² + g(y); then F<sub>y</sub> = x² + 2xy + g′(y) = N gives g′ = 0. Solution: x²y + xy² = C. (b) Solve (3xy + y²)dx + (x² + xy)dy = 0. Now M<sub>y</sub> = 3x + 2y and N<sub>x</sub> = 2x + y, not equal. Compute (M<sub>y</sub> − N<sub>x</sub>)/N = (x + y)/(x² + xy) = 1/x, a function of x alone, so μ = e<sup>∫dx/x</sup> = x. Multiply through: (3x²y + xy²)dx + (x³ + x²y)dy = 0, and now M<sub>y</sub> = 3x² + 2xy = N<sub>x</sub>. F = x³y + x²y²/2, so the solution is x³y + x²y²/2 = C.
chapters.trap: The test crosses the variables: differentiate M with respect to y and N with respect to x. Using M<sub>x</sub> and N<sub>y</sub> marks almost everything as inexact. And an integrating factor multiplies both M and N; multiplying only one leaves the equation inexact.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 to 1.3, plus partial derivatives and the idea of a total differential.
chapters.leave: Total differential (Pfaffian) equations in three variables belong to Unit 4; this chapter stays with two variables.

chapters.idea: For y′ + P(x)y = Q(x), multiplying by the integrating factor e<sup>∫P dx</sup> makes the left side the derivative of a single product, so one integration finishes the job.
chapters.depth: Define P and Q as continuous functions on the interval of interest and write the standard form with coefficient 1 on y′. Derive the integrating factor: multiplying by IF gives IF·y′ + P·IF·y, and the product rule needs (IF)′ = P·IF, that is IF = e<sup>∫P dx</sup>, meaning any one antiderivative, no constant. Then (y·IF)′ = Q·IF and y = IF<sup>−1</sup>(∫Q·IF dx + C). Some syllabi call this Leibnitz's linear equation; the same chapter heading is first-order linear equation. Work three examples: dy/dx + 2y = e<sup>−x</sup>; x dy/dx + 2y = x², which must be divided by x first; and one application, an RL circuit L di/dt + Ri = E(t) with numbers, or a brine-mixing tank. Add a short section on reduction to linear form: an equation of the shape f′(y)dy/dx + P(x)f(y) = Q(x) is linear in the unknown f(y), so solve for f(y) and invert. State clearly that Bernoulli's equation is the main case of this reduction and is handled in 1.6.

figure.title: The integrating factor
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom pipeline builds the integrating factor, multiplies, writes the left side as one derivative, and integrates.

chapters.example: Solve x dy/dx + 2y = x² with y(1) = 1. Divide by x: dy/dx + (2/x)y = x, so P = 2/x and Q = x. IF = e<sup>∫(2/x)dx</sup> = e<sup>2ln x</sup> = x². Then (y·x²)′ = x·x² = x³, so yx² = x⁴/4 + C and y = x²/4 + C/x². At x = 1, y = 1 gives 1 = 1/4 + C, so C = 3/4 and y = x²/4 + 3/(4x²).
chapters.trap: The equation must be in standard form first. In x y′ + 2y = x² the coefficient of y is 2, not 2/x — divide by x before reading off P. The sign of P goes inside the integral: y′ − 3y = 1 has IF = e<sup>−3x</sup>, not e<sup>3x</sup>.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 for the integrals, 1.4 for where the integrating-factor idea comes from.
chapters.leave: The yⁿ right side is 1.6. Second-order linear equations with constant coefficients are Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Bernoulli's equation y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)yⁿ becomes a linear equation under z = y<sup>1−n</sup>.
chapters.depth: Write the form, with n any real number other than 0 and 1: n = 0 is linear and n = 1 is separable, so both belong to earlier chapters. Divide through by yⁿ, substitute z = y<sup>1−n</sup>, so z′ = (1 − n)y<sup>−n</sup>y′, and obtain the linear equation z′ + (1 − n)P(x)z = (1 − n)Q(x). Solve it by the method of 1.5, then put z = y<sup>1−n</sup> back and simplify. Work two examples, one with n = 2 and one with a negative n such as n = −1, so the student sees the sign of (1 − n) change. Note the lost solution y = 0 when n > 0. One line of history-free naming: the same family name appears in fluid mechanics for a different equation, and that one is not in this unit.

figure.title: Bernoulli to linear
figure.aria: A left-to-right pipeline shows a Bernoulli equation turned into a linear equation in z, then back to y.

chapters.example: Solve x dy/dx + y = x²y². Divide by x: dy/dx + y/x = x y², so n = 2, P = 1/x, Q = x. Put z = y<sup>−1</sup>, so z′ = −y<sup>−2</sup>y′ and the equation becomes z′ − z/x = −x. IF = e<sup>−∫dx/x</sup> = 1/x, so (z/x)′ = −1 and z/x = −x + C, giving z = Cx − x². Since z = 1/y, the solution is 1/y = Cx − x², that is y = 1/(Cx − x²).
chapters.trap: Divide by yⁿ before substituting, and keep the factor (1 − n) on both P and Q. For n > 0 the division loses y = 0, which is a genuine solution. Do not apply the method to n = 0 or n = 1 — those are just the linear and separable cases.
chapters.prereq: 1.5 (the substitution produces a linear equation solved there), plus 1.2.
chapters.leave: Second-order and higher-order linear equations, with the Wronskian and particular integrals, are Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A first-order initial value problem has a solution near x₀ when f is continuous, and that solution is unique when f is also Lipschitz in y; Picard's iteration builds it by repeated integration.
chapters.depth: Define the initial value problem y′ = f(x, y), y(x₀) = y₀ and its geometry: a curve through the point (x₀, y₀) whose slope at every point is f. State Peano's existence theorem: continuity of f on a rectangle R = {|x − x₀| ≤ a, |y − y₀| ≤ b} alone guarantees at least one solution on |x − x₀| ≤ h with h = min(a, b/M) and M the maximum of |f| on R. State the Lipschitz condition |f(x, y<sub>1</sub>) − f(x, y<sub>2</sub>)| ≤ L|y<sub>1</sub> − y<sub>2</sub>|, show that a bounded ∂f/∂y gives L, and give one example that fails it: f = √y at y = 0. State Picard's theorem: continuous plus Lipschitz gives existence and uniqueness. Show non-uniqueness with y′ = √y, y(0) = 0, which has both y = 0 and y = x²/4. Show non-existence with y′ = 1/x, y(0) = 1, where f is undefined at the initial point. Give the Picard iteration y<sub>n+1</sub>(x) = y₀ + ∫<sub>x₀</sub><sup>x</sup> f(t, y<sub>n</sub>(t))dt starting from y₀(x) = y₀, run three steps, and say that the limit is the unique solution. Close with a short box on numerical solution, since some syllabi examine it in this unit: Euler's step y<sub>n+1</sub> = y<sub>n</sub> + h f(x<sub>n</sub>, y<sub>n</sub>), and the fourth-order Runge-Kutta step as the weighted average (k<sub>1</sub> + 2k<sub>2</sub> + 2k<sub>3</sub> + k<sub>4</sub>)/6 of four slopes, with one worked step and no error analysis.

figure.aria: Picard iterates 1, 1+x and 1+x+x²/2 close in on the exact curve e to the x between x = 0 and 1.5.

chapters.example: For y′ = y, y(0) = 1, compute Picard iterates and check the theorem. Here f(x, y) = y is continuous everywhere and ∂f/∂y = 1, so |f(x, y<sub>1</sub>) − f(x, y<sub>2</sub>)| = |y<sub>1</sub> − y<sub>2</sub>| and L = 1. Start with y₀(x) = 1. Then y<sub>1</sub> = 1 + ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>x</sup>1 dt = 1 + x; y<sub>2</sub> = 1 + ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>x</sup>(1 + t)dt = 1 + x + x²/2; y<sub>3</sub> = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6. The pattern is the Taylor polynomial of e<sup>x</sup>, so the iterates converge to y = e<sup>x</sup>. On the rectangle |x| ≤ 1, |y − 1| ≤ 1 we have a = 1, b = 1, M = 2, so the theorem promises a unique solution at least for |x| ≤ min(1, 1/2) = 0.5.
chapters.trap: Continuity alone gives existence, not uniqueness — that is Peano's theorem. Uniqueness needs the Lipschitz condition, and a solution can be unique yet exist only on a smaller interval than you expect, so quote h = min(a, b/M) with M taken on the rectangle. Also start the iteration from the constant y₀(x) = y₀, not from f.
chapters.prereq: 1.1, safe integration of simple functions, and the idea of a sequence of functions approaching a limit.
chapters.leave: Power series solutions and their radius of convergence are Unit 3; full numerical methods with error estimates belong to a numerical methods course, and linear equations of second order to Unit 2.
